question: Why Isn't Address Autocomplete Working at Checkout?
metaDescription: Usually a missing or invalid API key for the address-lookup service, or the field's JavaScript conflicting with another script on the page.
shortAnswer: Address autocomplete at checkout is typically powered by a third-party service (Google Places API, or a dedicated address-lookup plugin), and it depends on a valid, correctly configured API key with the right service enabled and billing set up on the provider's side — a missing, expired, or restricted API key is the most common single cause of it silently not working at all.

bodyHtml:
Why This Happens

Address autocomplete isn't something WooCommerce or a plugin can provide entirely on its own — it calls out to an external address-lookup service (most commonly Google's Places API) that requires its own account, enabled billing, and a valid API key configured specifically for that use. Any break in that chain, from an expired key to a service not enabled on the provider's console, will silently stop autocomplete from working without necessarily showing an obvious error on the checkout page itself.

Common Causes

  • An invalid, expired, or missing API key in the plugin's settings — this is the single most common cause and worth checking first.
  • API key restrictions (domain restrictions, specific API restrictions) configured on the provider's side not matching the actual live domain, which can silently block requests even with a technically valid key.
  • Billing not enabled on the Google Cloud (or equivalent) account tied to the API key — many address-lookup APIs require billing to be active even within a free usage tier.
  • A JavaScript conflict from another plugin or theme script interfering with the autocomplete library's initialization.
  • Usage quota exceeded for the API key, which can happen gradually as traffic grows and go unnoticed until autocomplete stops functioning.

How to Fix It

  1. Check the browser console for API-related errors when interacting with the address field, since the provider's own JavaScript usually logs a specific reason for failure there.
  2. Verify the API key is valid, unrestricted for the live domain, and has billing enabled on the provider's console.
  3. Check usage quotas to rule out the key simply having hit its limit.
  4. Test with a fresh, unrestricted key temporarily to isolate whether the issue is key-related or a broader JavaScript conflict.
